passages.title: The Heat Beneath the City
passages.text:
A  On a still summer night, the centre of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the fields beyond its edge. The difference is usually greatest three or four hours after sunset, when rural surfaces have already shed their heat but masonry and asphalt are still releasing what they absorbed during the day. This phenomenon is known as the urban heat island, and it is one of the most thoroughly documented consequences of urbanisation. It is also, in important respects, a matter of design rather than of climate: two cities beneath the same sky can differ by several degrees because of the way their streets, roofs and open spaces are arranged.

B  The physical causes are well understood. Dark materials such as asphalt and slate absorb a high proportion of incoming solar radiation and reflect relatively little, so a city's albedo — the fraction of light it bounces back — is lower than that of grassland or forest. Vegetation cools the air by evapotranspiration, drawing water from the soil and releasing it through leaves; where trees and gardens are replaced by paving, this natural air-conditioning disappears. Tall buildings add a third effect. They trap radiation between them, and narrow streets limit the movement of air, so heat that would otherwise be carried away lingers at ground level. Vehicles, factories and air-conditioning units contribute a fourth: waste heat discharged directly into the streets.

C  Thermal mass explains why the effect peaks after dark. Concrete, brick and stone conduct heat slowly, storing it through the afternoon and giving it up for hours after the sun has gone. Rural ground, by contrast, cools quickly once direct sunlight is removed. The result is a temperature gap that widens at night and can persist until dawn. Because the gap is widest when people are trying to sleep, it has consequences for health that are easily overlooked. It also complicates measurement: satellites record the temperature of surfaces, not of the air, and a roof in direct sunshine may be twenty degrees hotter than the air a metre above it.

D  The health effects fall unevenly. Heat stress and cardiovascular strain are greatest among older people and those already suffering from illness, and upper-floor flats in poorly insulated blocks can remain dangerously warm throughout the night. In many cities the districts with the least tree cover are also the poorest, a pattern documented in surveys from North America to South Asia. Residents there pay more to cool their homes, and some cannot afford to do so at all. Energy demand rises in step with temperature, which increases emissions and reinforces the problem, while water running off hot streets can raise the temperature of streams and rivers enough to harm fish.

E  Responses fall into two broad categories: reducing the heat that enters, and increasing the heat that leaves. Reflective 'cool' roofs and lighter-coloured pavements raise the albedo and can lower indoor temperatures markedly, although bright surfaces may cause glare and offer little benefit in winter. Trees and green roofs provide shade and evaporative cooling at the same time, but they need water and time to become established, and in dense districts there may be nowhere to plant them. Parks, ponds and permeable surfaces help, particularly when they are linked into networks rather than left as isolated patches. No single measure works everywhere in the same way.

F  Planning decisions often matter more than individual buildings. Street orientation determines whether a canyon is ventilated by the prevailing wind or sealed against it, and the height and spacing of blocks determine how much sky a pavement sees at noon. Several cities now require developers to model a project's effect on local temperatures before permission is granted, and a few have adopted canopy targets that specify a minimum proportion of tree cover by a given date. Such rules are easier to announce than to enforce, since canopy takes decades to develop and is vulnerable to drought, disease and the pressure to widen roads.

G  Yet the underlying lesson is encouraging. Because urban heat is largely a product of surfaces and layout, it can be altered by decisions that lie within the control of local government: what is planted, what is built and what is painted white. Cities that have measured the problem carefully, district by district, have generally found that the cheapest gains come from shade and ventilation — the oldest tools of urban design, rediscovered under a new name.

passages.title: How Paper Travelled West
passages.text:
A  Paper is so ordinary that its history is rarely examined, yet for more than a thousand years it was the cheapest and most adaptable surface on which to write. Earlier civilisations used clay tablets, stone, bamboo slips and papyrus, and medieval Europe relied on parchment, made from animal skin, which was durable but extremely expensive: a single large Bible could consume the skins of a small herd. The invention of paper is Chinese. Fragments recovered from a tomb at Fangmatan in Gansu province have been dated to the second century BCE, several hundred years before the date traditionally associated with the craft. Chinese accounts credit Cai Lun, a court official, with improving the technique in 105 CE by using tree bark, hemp, rags and old fishing nets; whether he invented the process or standardised an existing one, his name became attached to it.

B  The essential insight was to break plant fibres down in water and then reassemble them as a mat. Hemp, linen rags, mulberry bark and later bamboo were soaked, boiled and beaten into a pulp. A mould — a wooden frame fitted with a fine screen — was dipped into a vat of this pulp and lifted out flat, leaving a thin layer of fibres on the mesh. The sheet was pressed to squeeze out water and then hung to dry. Sizing, made from starch or gelatin, was brushed on afterwards to prevent ink from bleeding into the fibres.

C  Paper travelled east before it travelled west. Buddhist monks carried it to Korea and Japan, where local plants gave rise to distinctive traditions: Korean hanji, made from mulberry, and Japanese washi, valued for its strength and translucency. The westward route was slower and less peaceful. According to tradition, papermakers were among the craftsmen taken from China to Samarkand after a battle in 751, and the craft reached Baghdad within a century. Mills followed in Damascus, Cairo and Fez, supplying administrators, scholars and merchants across the Islamic world.

D  Europe acquired paper through the Iberian peninsula, where a mill was operating at Xàtiva by the eleventh century, and through Italy, where the town of Fabriano became the continent's most innovative centre. Its craftsmen replaced manual beating with water-powered hammers, introduced animal glue sizing and developed the watermark, a design formed by wire sewn onto the screen. These marks identified the maker and, incidentally, allow historians to date undated books. Paper was now far cheaper than parchment, but it was still made from linen rags, and the supply of rags — collected door to door by traders — set a ceiling on production.

E  The printing press transformed the economics of the industry. Movable type had existed in East Asia for centuries, but the combination of a press, oil-based ink and a plentiful supply of paper in fifteenth-century Europe made mass production possible. Demand rose so sharply that mills multiplied along rivers, which provided both the water power for stamping and the water needed for the pulp. By 1500 presses in more than two hundred European towns had produced an estimated twenty million volumes, and the price of books had fallen far enough for ordinary merchants to own them.

F  The nineteenth century brought two changes that still shape the material. In 1803 a machine financed by the Fourdrinier brothers and built by Bryan Donkin produced paper as a continuous web rather than one sheet at a time, and wood replaced rags as the principal source of fibre after methods of grinding and chemically pulping timber were developed. Paper became cheap enough for newspapers with circulations in the hundreds of thousands. The gain had a hidden cost. Groundwood pulp retains lignin, and paper sized with alum forms acids as it ages, so much nineteenth- and twentieth-century paper has yellowed and turned brittle; libraries now spend large sums on deacidification and on copying volumes that are crumbling on the shelf.

G  Paper remains a bulk commodity, with global production of roughly four hundred million tonnes a year. The decline of newspapers in wealthy countries has been offset by the growth of packaging, and recycling now supplies a substantial share of fibre in Europe and North America. Whether that balance holds depends less on technology than on regulation: restrictions on single-use plastic have increased demand for paper bags and wraps, while concerns about forestry and water use push manufacturers towards certification and closed-loop mills. The material that began as a way of reusing rags has become, once again, an exercise in reuse.

passages.title: What the Sleeping Brain Rehearses
passages.text:
A  Sleep occupies roughly a third of human life, yet for most of the twentieth century it was treated as a passive condition, a switch that turned consciousness off until morning. That view has been replaced by something far more active. Recordings from inside the sleeping brain show patterns of activity that resemble those of learning itself, and the proteins that build connections between neurons are synthesised in greater quantities during sleep than during waking. Sleep is not, however, a single state. It alternates between rapid-eye-movement (REM) sleep and three stages of non-REM sleep, in cycles of about ninety minutes. Slow-wave sleep, the deepest stage, is concentrated in the first half of the night, while REM periods lengthen towards morning.

B  The first experimental hint of a link with memory came in 1924, when two American psychologists, Jenkins and Dallenbach, asked students to learn lists of nonsense syllables and then either sleep or stay awake for the same interval. Retention was markedly better after sleep. The result was striking but hard to interpret, because sleep was then regarded as one undifferentiated state; the researchers could not say which part of it mattered. The discovery of REM sleep by Aserinsky and Kleitman in 1953, and the arrival of brain imaging half a century later, made it possible to ask more precise questions.

C  The strongest evidence concerns declarative memory — facts and events that can be stated in words. During slow-wave sleep, cells in the hippocampus, the structure that first encodes such memories, repeat the sequences of activity recorded during learning. These replays coincide with brief, high-frequency bursts known as sharp-wave ripples, and with slow oscillations in the cortex that appear to coordinate the transfer of information between the two regions. The link is not merely correlational. In a much-cited experiment, volunteers learned the positions of cards on a screen while a particular odour was present; when the same odour was released during slow-wave sleep, their memory for the positions improved, and the effect disappeared when the cue was presented while they were awake.

D  Procedural skills — riding a bicycle, typing, playing a scale — follow a different and less tidy pattern. Many studies report that performance improves overnight without further practice, and some attribute this to REM sleep, during which the brain is chemically and electrically close to waking. Yet the evidence is less consistent than the declarative findings. Improvement has been observed after naps containing no REM, and people who take antidepressant drugs that suppress REM sleep do not display the memory deficits a simple theory would predict. Stage 2 sleep, with its bursts of activity called spindles, now seems at least as important for motor learning as REM does.

E  Spindles deserve attention in their own right. They are short trains of waves at eleven to sixteen hertz, generated in the thalamus, and their density varies widely between individuals and declines with age. Several studies have found that people with more frequent spindles retain more of what they learned the previous day, and that spindle density predicts improvement on some tasks. Naps of sixty to ninety minutes, long enough to include slow-wave sleep, have produced measurable gains in both declarative and procedural tests, although the effects are usually modest and do not appear in every study.

F  Sleep may also perform an emotional function. REM sleep is the only state in which certain stress-related chemicals are almost absent, and imaging studies show that the amygdala, a region central to fear, is less reactive after a night of sleep than after an equivalent period of waking. This has led to the popular claim that REM provides 'overnight therapy', stripping the emotion from difficult memories while preserving their content. The claim is attractive, but the experiments behind it are small and the results have not always been replicated; what can be said is that sleep loss reliably raises emotional reactivity, whatever the mechanism.

G  For students, the practical message is less glamorous than the headlines suggest. Sleep deprivation impairs the hippocampus's ability to encode new material, so a night spent revising is likely to cost more in learning than it gains in hours. Later school start times have been followed by improved attendance and grades in several districts, though such studies are difficult to disentangle from other changes. What the research does not support is the idea of sleep as a download: consolidation is selective, it favours information that is relevant or rewarded, and much of the underlying biology remains uncertain. The most defensible advice is also the oldest — keep regular hours, and do not treat sleep as time that can be borrowed without repayment.

questions.explanation: Đoạn 5 (E) chỉ nêu giấc ngủ trưa 60–90 phút mang lại lợi ích đo được; bài không so sánh với một đêm ngủ đầy đủ.

questions.prompt: Some popular accounts of sleep research claim more than the evidence supports.
questions.explanation: Đoạn 6 (F) và đoạn 7 (G) cho rằng các tuyên bố phổ biến như 'overnight therapy' hay ngủ như một bản tải về vượt quá bằng chứng hiện có.
